analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income taxes with a flat 10% tax on wages, while corporations, investments, and estates pay nothing.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Philip Crane with no cosponsors, died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out almost the entire federal tax system as it existed in 2003 and replace it with a single 10% tax on earned income — money people make from working. Wages above a $10,000-per-person exemption would be taxed, but income from investments (capital gains, interest, most dividends), pensions, and corporate profits would be taxed at zero. It would also erase the estate and gift taxes and cancel all unpaid federal income tax debts from years before 2002, except taxes tied to illegal activity. At the same time, it would strike every deduction, exclusion, and credit in the individual income tax code.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations, which would pay no income tax at all; holders of investment wealth, whose capital gains, interest, and dividends would be untaxed; retirees living on pensions, which are excluded from the tax base; and anyone with unpaid federal income tax from before 2002, whose debt would be wiped clean. Large estates would also escape the estate tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations and households living on investments

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the corporate income tax and a dozen related corporate taxes outright, so corporations would owe no federal income tax [S2][S3].

The new individual tax applies only to 'earned income' — wages, salaries, and self-employment earnings. Capital gains, interest, rents, most dividends, and pension or annuity income are not earned income, so they would be taxed at zero [S3].
The bill repeals the entire estate, gift, and generation-skipping tax subtitle, so large inherited fortunes would pass untaxed [S2][S3].

It grants amnesty for all federal income tax liability for taxable years ending before January 1, 2002, canceling unpaid taxes, penalties, and interest except those tied to illegal business activity [S2][S3].
The first $10,000 of earned income per person (adjusted for inflation) would be exempt, which would fully shield some low earners from the tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Working people, who would bear essentially the entire individual tax burden through a flat 10% tax on their pay, while losing every deduction and credit — including the earned income tax credit and child credits that supplement low wages. The federal government would also lose the bulk of its income tax revenue, leaving less money for public services or a much larger deficit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wage earners who lose all deductions and credits

drawbacks.text: Repealing the corporate tax, the estate and gift taxes, and all taxes on investment income would eliminate most of the federal revenue base, leaving a 10% wage tax that could not cover government spending without deep cuts or historically large deficits [S2][S3].
Striking 'all deductions and all credits' would end the earned income tax credit, child credits, and education credits that millions of working families rely on to supplement low wages [S2][S3].

The blanket amnesty would wipe out every unpaid income tax debt from before 2002, rewarding those who never paid while everyone else did, with an exception only for taxes tied to illegal activity [S3].

A flat 10% tax treats a cashier's paycheck and a surgeon's salary identically and taxes no unearned income at all, shifting the overall tax burden toward people who work for a living and away from those who live on wealth [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow almost entirely to corporations, investors, and large estates, while the cost — both the 10% wage tax with no offsets and the collapse of federal revenue — falls on working people and anyone who depends on federal spending. It is a large transfer from wage earners to holders of capital, wrapped in a flat-rate 'tithe' framing that also gives a small break to the lowest earners.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, drew no cosponsors, and died there when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the bill on April 11, 2003, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee never reported the bill, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Working taxpayers came out ahead: the proposed shift of nearly the whole tax load onto wages — with corporations, investments, and estates paying nothing — never advanced, and the existing tax structure stayed in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers who would have borne the shift

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; no other member joined him.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it never received a hearing or markup and was never reported to the floor.

against.name: House Members
against.what_they_did: Not one member added their name as a cosponsor over the bill's lifetime.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan split is visible in the record beyond the Republican sponsor's lone support.

industries.note: The bill repeals the corporate income tax and a dozen related corporate levies outright, so corporations would owe no federal income tax while their owners' capital income goes untaxed too. The revenue they stop contributing would have to come from wage earners or borrowing [S3].

Because the tax applies only to earned income, capital gains, interest, rents, and most dividends would be taxed at zero, while wages are taxed at 10%. This sharply shifts the tax burden away from wealth and onto paychecks [S3].

industries.industry: Insurance companies, REITs, and investment funds
industries.note: The bill specifically repeals taxes on life insurers, mutual insurers, regulated investment companies, and real estate investment trusts [S3].
Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes lets multi-million-dollar inheritances pass untaxed [S2][S3].
Amnesty cancels all pre-2002 income tax debts, penalties, and interest, letting people who never paid walk away while compliant taxpayers' past payments stand [S3].
